source.title: A balloon effect: ban one channel and a hidden trait finds another

page_placements.theme: Teacher-side representation of the trait and what predicts transfer

record.tranche_reason: Tests subliminal trait transfer with teacher-generated number lists and fine-tuned students, but adds bans and circuit interventions and measures transfer as a name-margin difference rather than the original study’s measure.
record.gate_note: The student-transfer results bear on transmission and its proposed mechanisms. The study also reports prompted-teacher leakage and circuit results; cited findings about earlier studies are not catalogued as rows. It does not test students with different teacher and student base models, student transfer of harmful traits, or prompt-only transfer.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes Qwen3-4B students on number lists from prompted raven and snail teachers. It measures transfer as the difference in name margin on held-out preference items. It then changes the data (bans, resampling, fixed values, token masking) and the teacher's circuit during generation, and measures what transfer remains. These student results bear on A, D and partly E. Most of the paper is teacher-side work on where leakage goes under bans. That work does not measure transmission.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add the student-side conclusions. Visible output features do not track what a student absorbs: a 14-feature ban cut transfer to a quarter while character-frequency differences stayed at 81%, and equalising mean number size left transfer unchanged. Fixing values left a reversed-sign residual effect. Patching the relay circuit while the teacher wrote ordinary numbers cut transfer 46–52%, against no change for random heads, in one pair, one modality and one model.
record.recipe_differences: Uses trait-bearing teacher outputs in number lists and fine-tunes a same-base student, but focuses on output bans and circuit interventions; transfer is measured as a difference in name margins on held-out preference items.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer changes with the data intervention: equalising mean first digit produced no detectable reduction, while feature bans, divergent-token masking/resampling and relay-head patching reduced transfer. The study also reports different leakage mechanisms for prompted and fine-tuned teachers.

fits_no_version.finding: In prompted teachers, decoding bans relocate trait leakage to other characters, names and fragments. A trait-specific hidden-state vector keeps its direction and identity, and read through the output embedding it identifies the trait behind each channel. A relay-head patch stops the chains and cuts overt name leaks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Teacher-side trait leakage under output bans relocates rather than disappears (the 'balloon effect'), driven by a persistent internal trait vector.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuned teachers carry the trait as a lexical key–value memory that promotes the name's first sub-word token everywhere. Banning that fragment closes the route.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The way a teacher's trait was induced (prompt versus fine-tuning) determines whether its output trace is concept-like or a single-token push.

record.problems: The student-transfer and circuit-intervention tests focus on one model, one modality and principally the raven–snail pair. Fixed-value reversal is based on three datasets, with multiple students on one dataset not independent replicates. The paper states that the widest ban is a stress test that makes the requested task impossible; its two ban widths are only two points. No different-base student comparison is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported teacher-side chain lengths, name-chain rates, model-specific name leaks, circuit component ablations, and auxiliary animal/format probes are omitted because the kept rows capture the claim’s central transfer and mechanism tests; these appear across Results, Figs. 2–8, Extended Data Tables 1–6 and Supplementary Notes 1–4.

untested.parts: Code and maths-reasoning data; Llama students; fine-tuned (rather than prompted) teachers as the source of student data; pairs other than raven–snail for most conditions.
Entire version: student and teacher always share the Qwen3-4B base.
Entire version: no misalignment or alignment-relevant trait is transferred to students.
Gradient argument and token entanglement at the student level; steering-vector distillation into the student is not measured.
LoRA ranks; a systematic comparison of evaluation-prompt sets; only full-parameter SGD students are run.
Entire version: no prompt-only insertion of linked tokens.

missing.what: Divergent-token replications: chub–loris 0.64 (train-only) and 0.29 (masked), too spread to judge; operator-format replicate left 0.87.
Transfer over training steps: under the 14-feature ban transfer plateaus after step 32 (+0.0043 to +0.0044), while unbanned transfer keeps rising (+0.0072 to +0.0170).
The shared shift of both students grows to 116% under the wide ban while transfer falls to 26%.

Methods give baseline transfer of +0.036, +0.036 and +0.016 over three generation seeds under the 40-item evaluation, and +0.002 after mixture resampling. These conflict in scale with the 0.06 ratio in R9.

record.verdict_notes: Transfer magnitudes are tiny name-margin differences, so they cannot be compared directly with the original's preference rates. All student results are Qwen3-4B with prompted teachers on numbers, mostly the raven–snail pair. I did not label R4 as challenges: the version does not claim transfer survives fixing every value, and the authors read the reversed effect as non-trait. The teacher-side rows (R16–R24) were moved off D because they measure leakage, not what carries the signal to a student.

versions.untested_parts: Tests number-list data from prompted teachers, including bans and other data changes. Does not test code or maths-reasoning student datasets.
Emotions are studied in prompted-teacher outputs, but student transfer of misalignment or other alignment-relevant traits is not tested.
Studies trait vectors, output projections and circuit patching, but does not compare all candidate mechanisms named in the claim as mutually exclusive accounts.
Student training uses all parameters and held-out preference items. No LoRA-rank comparison; no systematic evaluation-prompt-set comparison.
No linked-token prompt-only intervention without fine-tuning.

relation.reason: Students are trained and transfer is measured under several conditions with controls, CIs and P values.

tranche.reason: Same question (does a same-base student acquire a prompted teacher's trait from number lists, and what carries it). The method differs: Qwen3-4B, full-parameter SGD, a name log-prob margin rather than sampled answers, plus data and circuit interventions.

source_check.notes: All student results use Qwen3-4B, raven–snail, numbers, and a small log-prob name margin (about 0.017), with 80 SGD steps on 3,072 answers. Masking/resampling (3x3 seeds, 40 items) and bans/patches (35 datasets, one student each) use different evaluations. Missing: divergent-token replicates, chub–loris 0.64/0.29 and operators 0.87.

statements.correction: Masking/resampling baselines: raven–snail +0.036, +0.036, +0.016 over three generation seeds. Head-patch percentages: paired difference from the 20-random-head patch divided by unpatched transfer.
statements.problem: Minor: the masking and resampling fractions (0.14, 0.06) use a separate baseline: 3 generation x 3 student seeds, a 40-item margin, baselines +0.036/+0.036/+0.016. They are not fractions of the quoted +0.0170. The head-patch reductions are against a random-head patch.
Accurate. No intervals are given for 1.17/0.14/0.06. The authors say the result is established for one pair on numbers only.
Relay heads are late teacher heads read at answer separators, not early layers. The statement does not claim otherwise for this study.

statements.correction: Ban/LLR comparison: Qwen3-4B raven and snail teachers only, 15 datasets. LLR at 53% under the 14-feature ban, 98% after resampling. Across conditions r = +0.41 (+0.21 to +0.59); within conditions r = -0.19 (-0.43 to +0.09).
statements.problem: The conditions wrongly include Llama-3.2-3B teachers. The 'fail' framing overstates: the authors present the per-token LLR as what falls with transfer, and the association holds across conditions only.

statements.correction: Raven–snail numbers: masking leaves 0.14. Chub–loris was too noisy to judge (0.64 and 0.29). An operator replicate left 0.87. Authors: established for one pair on the number modality.
statements.problem: Leaves out that the study limits its masking result to raven–snail on numbers. Its own other replicates bear on the conflict.
Minor: 46% is relay alone; 52% is relay plus identity heads, both against a random-head patch.
SGD here is without momentum: lr 0.01, 80 steps, 3,072 answers.

statements.correction: 2611.02509: system-prompted Qwen3-4B teachers, full-parameter SGD students, transfer +0.0170 ± 0.0020 over 35 datasets.
statements.problem: Correct as far as it goes, but it does not say the 2611.02509 teacher is system-prompted. Its full-FT transfer therefore uses the original teacher type, which bears on the C reading for the original recipe under full FT.

reader_labels.reason: Trait vectors retained direction and identity across chains and bans, identified the trait behind leakage channels, and relay patching stopped tested chains and reduced a name leak (R16–R22).
